Kabīr
(A. D. 1440-1518)
------------------------------------------
One of the great leaders of the भक्ति Movement and a pioneer of Hindu-Muslim unity, Kabīr—also known as Kabīrdās—was brought up as an adopted child by the Muslim weaver couple Nīru and Nīmā who had found him abandoned near a tank. From the childhood days, he was of a devotional and philosophical temperament. He cleverly managed to become a disciple of the great saint of the times, रामानन्द of the Vaiṣṇava sect, who later accepted him wholeheartedly.
KabīrdasHe had also come under the influence of Gosāi Aṣṭāvand.
His adopting Hindu ways of life brought him into conflict with the contemporary Muslim society. But very soon, everybody had to concede that he was a saint, a man of God, who had transcended all social and religio-cultural barriers.
Kabīr was married to Lori and had a son, Kamāl who was also a saint.
Kabīr is said to have passed away in Maghar (now in Pakistan). When the Muslims and Hindus were quarelling over the disposal of the dead body, they are said to have found a heap of flowers below the shroud! This was equally shared by them to be disposed off according to their respective customs. The result was a Mandir and a Mausoleum side by side.
Kabīr has composed hundreds of songs mostly in the Avadhi and Bhojpurī languages. They are compositions containing the natural outpourings of the heart of a saint, of a realised सोउल्. His philosophy as reflected in these songs may be summarized as follows: God is one only, for all the people of the world. There is no need to worship him through symbols and icons. The path to God is open to all, without any distinction of caste, colour or sex. The path of devotion is universal and is equally open to the Hindus as well as the Muslims. In the spiritual path, guidance from a competent गुरु or teacher is a must. All devotional literature must be in simple local vernaculars.
The followers of कबीर् gradually evolved into a separate sect known as ‘Kabīrpanthis’ within the Hindu fold.
Scholars are of the opinion that कबीर् had influenced गुरु Nānak (A. D. 1469-1539) and Dādu (A. D. 1544-1603), two more well-known teachers of the भक्ति Movement.
Kabīr’s compositions have been compiled into a work called Bījak, as early as A. D. 1570.
His works are now available in the following forms: Kabīr Sāhabkī Śabdāvalī, Kabīranke Pad, Sākhiyā, Kabīr Vacanā-valī and Kabīr Granthāvalī.

Kabandha
(‘headless [demon]’)
------------------------------------------
An interesting interlude in the story of the Rāmāyaṇa is that of कबन्ध. He was a headless demon with two very long arms and a mouth inside his abdomen. A gandharva (a class of semigods), Viśvāvasu by name, he had incurred the wrath of the sage Sthūlaśiras and had been cursed by him to get this grotesque form. A blow on the head by इन्द्र with his वज्रायुध (thunderbolt) had made it worse.
When राम and लक्ष्मण were wandering in the दण्डक forest, searching for सीता, they were caught by him. However, when they cut his arms, he enquired who they were and was glad to get their identity since his लिबेरतिओन् from the curse was in राम’s hands. At his request राम and Lakśmaṇa killed him and cremated his body. Once the abominable body was destroyed, Viśvāvasu appeared and advised राम to contact सुग्रीव for help in locating and recovering सीता.
